chunks: Muḥammad ibn al-Fuḍayl narrated from Abū al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Kinānī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

He was asked about al-suknā and al-ʿumrā, and he said: “If he assigned the residential right during his lifetime, then it is according to the condition he stipulated. And if he assigned it to him and to his descendants after him until his descendants come to an end, then they have no right to sell the house, nor to pass it on by inheritance. Then the house returns to its first owner.”

key_terms.السُّكْنَى: A grant of residential use or right of dwelling
key_terms.الْعُمْرَى: A life estate-type grant tied to the lifetime of the beneficiary
key_terms.تُرْجَعُ الدَّارُ إِلَى صَاحِبِهَا الْأَ: The house returns to its original owner
key_terms.لَا يُورِثُوا الدَّارَ: They may not transfer the house through inheritance

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on sūknā and ʿumrā in Shia fiqh when a house is granted for residence or for descendants?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on conditional property grants such as residential right and life estate. It states that the grant follows the stipulated condition, and if it extends to a person's descendants, they may benefit from it but may not sell or inherit ownership of the house, which ultimately returns to its original owner.
